title: Swedish Rehn–Meidner policy complex, 1951–1983
summary: A bounded case of solidaristic wage bargaining, macroeconomic restraint, and labor-market adjustment used to examine distribution and coordination claims.

sources.title: The Rehn-Meidner Model in Sweden: Its Rise, Challenges and Survival
sources.authorityNote: Reconstructs the model, its instruments, periodization, incomplete implementation, and challenges.

sources.title: Wage differentials, economic restructuring and the solidaristic wage policy in Sweden
sources.authorityNote: Uses new wage data to separate the timing of compression and reassess its relationship to structural change.

sources.title: Wage Dispersion and Productive Efficiency: Evidence for Sweden
sources.authorityNote: Econometric evidence distinguishes interindustry from within-industry wage compression and their different productivity associations.

claims.text: Peak organizations negotiated solidaristic wage policy from 1956 until centralized bargaining broke down in 1983.
limitations: Dates bound the selected bargaining episode, not every component of Swedish economic policy.

claims.text: Wage inequality was stable before the late 1960s and declined rapidly thereafter; the 1970s decline was likely substantially related to deliberate union policy.
limitations: The study disputes a simple account of 1960s compression and does not identify one cause for all wage changes.

claims.text: Reduced interindustry wage differentials were associated with higher aggregate output and productivity, while within-industry compression was not.
limitations: An association in this period does not establish transferability or isolate every concurrent institution.

conflictingEvidence.summary: Molinder finds wage compression coincided with falling growth and structural change, qualifying broader claims that compression itself drove rapid restructuring; Hibbs and Locking find different results for interindustry and within-industry compression.

limitations: The policy model was never implemented consistently.
Postwar institutions and economic conditions limit transfer to other places and periods.

relationships.reason: The program arose within Swedish organized labor and social-democratic policymaking, without embodying the whole tradition.
The case provides evidence about wage distribution but not a complete answer about wealth or control.
The evidence requires separate treatment of wage, ownership, and productivity outcomes.

proposedRelationships.reason: Central wage frames and active labor-market adjustment are the institutional mechanism examined.

duplicateCandidates.reason: The tradition revision proposes this same companion case relationship; this file supplies the independently reviewable case entity.

content.name: Swedish Rehn–Meidner policy complex
content.scope: Begins with the 1951 LO program, focuses on the 1956–1982 centralized-bargaining window, and ends with the 1983 breakdown; excludes the later enacted wage-earner funds.
content.selectionRationale: Tests claims about coordinated bargaining, wage distribution, restructuring, and labor-market adjustment using a case with competing empirical findings.
conditions: Macroeconomic and labor-market policies operating alongside wage bargaining
outcomes: Different productivity associations for interindustry and within-industry compression
rivalExplanations: Economic structure, macroeconomic policy, wage drift, and shocks may explain outcomes attributed to solidaristic wage policy
transferLimitations: The institutional density and postwar setting were not generic
Observed wage compression cannot establish wealth redistribution or worker control
